title: Receive ye the Holy Ghost (John 20:19–23)
hook: he breathes on them: whose sins you forgive; the Church roots confession here

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene, apostle to the apostles. Your line was I have seen the lord. Who did you tell your good news to? Day five hundred thirty-two.

Sunday evening, the same day. Mary has told them what she saw. And where are the disciples? In a room with the doors shut, John says, for fear. Picture it: men who ran away three days ago, jumping at every footstep on the stairs, wondering if they're next, wondering what they'll say if he really is alive. Not a room full of faith. A room full of nerves and guilt. And then he's simply there, standing in the middle of them. The first thing he says is today's line.
screen: `DOORS SHUT, FOR FEAR.` → `MEN WHO RAN AWAY.` → `HE STANDS IN THE MIDST.`

segments.voice: He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Peace be to you." No accusation. No, where were you? He shows them his hands and his side, the opened side we looked at two days ago, and they're glad. Then he says it again, peace be to you, and adds: as the Father hath sent me, I also send you. And John records something strange and physical: "he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them: and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained." That word, breathed, is rare in the Greek Bible. In the Greek translation of Genesis, the same verb is used when God breathes the breath of life into the first human. Here, on the first day of a new week, Jesus breathes again, and many readers, ancient and modern, hear a new creation beginning. And the first thing the breath is for is forgiveness. Remember who's in the room. Men who denied him and ran. The first gift given to them is the power to forgive. The Catholic Church roots the sacrament of penance, confession, in this moment. The Council of Trent taught that here Christ gave the apostles and their successors the power to forgive and retain sins, and the Catechism cites this verse. That's why, in confession, the priest's words of absolution speak of the Holy Spirit sent among us for the forgiveness of sins, and of pardon and peace. And that's week seventy-six: I am he, not of this world, Ecce Homo, woman, blood and water, the apostle to the apostles, and the breath of peace.
screen: `PEACE BE TO YOU.` · `AS THE FATHER SENT ME.` · `HE BREATHED ON THEM.` · `THE ROOT OF CONFESSION.` · then, large: `RECEIVE YE THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe and receive peace. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow down by itself. Notice the air coming in, cool at the nose, and going out warm. If there's something you feel guilty about today, let it be there in the room with you, the way the disciples' failures were there. Don't argue with it. On each in-breath, imagine receiving peace. On each out-breath, let a little of the fear go. If you pray, you can hold Jesus's first words, peace be to you. If you don't, just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Breathed. The rare word for what the risen Jesus did to his frightened disciples, echoing the breath of life in Genesis, before sending them to forgive. Today's word.
Your line: peace be to you. Today, when someone who let you down walks in, let your first words be peaceful, before anything else. Day five hundred thirty-two.
screen: `WEEK SEVENTY-SIX: EGŌ EIMI · NOT OF THIS WORLD · ECCE HOMO · WOMAN · BLOOD AND WATER · APOSTLE · BREATH`

howItsDone: Catholics confess their sins to a priest in the sacrament of penance; the priest prays the words of absolution, which name the Holy Spirit sent for the forgiveness of sins, and sends the penitent away in peace.

fork.setup: you're the risen Jesus. the friends who abandoned you are hiding behind locked doors. you appear among them. what do you say first?
fork.reveal: peace be to you. then he shows them his wounds, sends them, breathes on them, and gives them the power to forgive.

trapdoor: what you thought: a blessing on a holiday.
what it means: the risen Jesus breathes new life into frightened failures, and sends them out to forgive.
what a scholar hears: enephysēsen appears in the Greek of Genesis 2:7; Trent (Session 14, canon 3) ties John 20:22–23 to penance; CCC 1441–1442 and 1485 cite it.
recall: lit in the temple court at the feast

notes: Emphysaō/enephysēsen used in LXX Genesis 2:7 and John 20:22 (its only New Testament use). Confirm.
Council of Trent, Session 14 (1551), ch. 1 and canon 3 on John 20:22–23. Confirm.
Absolution formula described, not quoted (current English translation under copyright). Confirm description.
'A new creation' reading of the breath (Gen 2:7 echo) is framed as how many readers hear it, not as settled exegesis.
'The same day' (20:19 'the same day at evening') and 'first day of a new week' are from the text. Confirm.
